---
title: "Discussion"
---

We conducted a longitudinal study of 2,491 participants (mean age 76 y) who were assessed twice, five years apart, and followed for up to 13.4 years. Over this age and time span we investigated the epigenetic signals that discriminated among six clinically defined stages, and how those signals changed along the clinical progression ordering, which runs from the earliest transition, normal2mci, through stable normal cognition to prevalent dementia (@tbl-dementia-category, Fig. [-@fig-normal2mci]–[-@fig-pathway-analysis]). We identified 403 CpG sites at *P* < 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ that were significantly associated with at least one stage. To identify broad patterns of latent methylation that differed by clinical stage, these 403 differentially methylated positions (DMPs) were analyzed with dimension reduction approaches. Two findings emerged: a continuous latent methylation trajectory aligned with clinical progression, and heterogeneity in the early-stage methylation profiles of participants with MCI.

### Dimension reduction

In each method, four of the six latent dimensions separated prevalent dementia from stable normal cognition (t-test, *P* < 1.0 × 10⁻²; @fig-vae-boxplots a, @suppfig-umap-boxplot-t8). Latent values decreased along the clinical ordering in the three VAE dimensions shown, VAE_6, VAE_2 and VAE_4; of the four UMAP dimensions shown, UMAP_1 and UMAP_5 increased and UMAP_2 decreased along the ordering, while UMAP_4 changed less consistently (@fig-vae-boxplots c-d). The dimensions carrying the progression signal were not the same across the two methods, and the sign of a latent axis is arbitrary, so the two approaches recapitulate the same structure rather than the same coordinates. This progression structure was graded across the six groups, as supported by the dementia progression score in most dimension pairs (@fig-vae-boxplots, @fig-scatter-peak, @suppfig-perm-heatmap). Because the variational autoencoder and UMAP rest on different mathematical foundations — one probabilistic, the other topological — their convergence strengthens the evidence that these patterns reflect biological signal rather than an artifact of any single method. The patterns also reappeared at the suggestive threshold *P* < 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ (949 CpG sites, more than twice the 403 retained at *P* < 1.0 × 10⁻⁸), indicating that the structure is not confined to the most significant sites.

APOE genotype tracked those progression axes (@fig-apoe-boxplots). Others have identified a role for APOE in modulating epigenetic changes [@RN92]. That the latent dimensions trained without any genotype information nonetheless ordered themselves by APOE role suggests that APOE-related and progression-related methylation variation are captured by the same latent axes. However, our data cannot determine whether APOE-associated methylation differences contribute to progression or merely co-vary with it.

### Genetic information

The 403 significant CpG sites annotated to a number of genes previously implicated in dementia (@suppfig-manhattan, @suppdata-DMP403). *NOTCH3* is implicated in the cerebral arteriopathy that underlies stroke and dementia [@RN45]; *BACE2* cleaves the amyloid-β protein precursor and may influence Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis [@RN46]; and *RAB7A* is integral to autophagosome-lysosome trafficking, affecting lysosomal maturation and protein aggregation in neurons [@RN48]. *GLP1R* encodes a transmembrane receptor with roles in insulin secretion, diabetes and obesity as well as in energy metabolism [@RN85; @RN91], and is of particular interest because GLP-1 receptor agonists have recently been tested in a trial with a dementia endpoint [@RN84]. Although APOE genotype tracked the latent dimensions, no CpG annotated to *APOE* itself reached genome-wide significance, as also reported in whole-genome methylation sequencing of blood in late-onset Alzheimer's disease [@RN39]. The genes annotated to these CpG sites were distributed across the genome rather than clustered at a few loci, which supports a systems-level rather than a single-locus approach to studying dementia.

### MCI findings

MCI has a heterogeneous clinical profile in which different cognitive domains may be affected [@RN94], and only a fraction of those given a clinical diagnosis of MCI go on to develop dementia [@RN95; @RN96]. The two MCI groups that did not progress to dementia — normal2mci and stable_mci — behaved differently from one another and from the groups that ended in dementia.

The stable_mci group was barely distinguishable from stable normal, with no VAE or UMAP dimension separating the two (@fig-vae-boxplots b, @suppfig-umap-boxplot-t8). At the single-CpG level it was also the only group to carry a cluster of outlying sites: 60 of the 403 DMPs had large negative effect sizes in stable_mci (effect size < −0.2) while sitting near zero in every other group and remaining uncorrelated with every transition (Supplementary Fig. [-@suppfig-stable_mci_DMP]–[-@suppfig-stable_mci_extended_transitions]). The same outlying cluster may be what places the stable_mci centroid off the progression path in the VAE latent space while UMAP keeps it on the path (@fig-scatter-peak e-h, Supplementary Fig. [-@suppfig-vae-scatter-t8-p1]–[-@suppfig-umap-scatter-t8-p2]). Understanding the role of this cluster could provide clues regarding the underlying biology or clinical presentations of the MCI group.

The normal2mci group differed from the others in the opposite way. In the pairwise correlations of DMP effect sizes, prevalent dementia was positively correlated with each of the groups that progressed to dementia but negatively correlated with normal2mci (@fig-normal2mci a-d). Participants who were cognitively normal at baseline therefore separated into two distinct groups: those who later progressed to dementia and already carried a baseline profile that aligned with prevalent dementia signatures, and those who progressed only to MCI, whose effects ran in the opposite direction (@fig-normal2mci, Supplementary Fig. [-@suppfig-normal2incid_DMP]–[-@suppfig-ES_corr_mci2incid_normal2mci]). The inversion persisted across CpG selection thresholds and across both analytic views that carry a direction — single-site effects and latent dimensions. In the latent space, normal2mci sits on the far side of stable normal from the dementia groups, which is the same signal seen at the single-CpG level rather than a contradiction of it. That the direction is reproduced at two levels of aggregation points to a coordinated, higher-order feature of the methylome rather than to the behavior of a few loci [@RN86; @RN97]. Together these findings suggest that biologically defined subtypes may exist within MCI. Such methylation signatures may be clinically useful for predicting future cognitive state, and may offer insight into the genetic and environmental factors that drive the heterogeneous presentations of mild cognitive impairment.

### Stage-specific biology

Our bioinformatic analyses and previous research suggested a temporal map of biological process engagement across dementia progression [@RN49; @RN50; @RN52; @RN53; @RN54; @RN55; @RN56; @RN57; @RN58; @RN59]. The earliest transition, normal2mci, was uniquely enriched for several functional categories — ion transport and regulation, synaptic function and organization, and extracellular matrix organization — that together reflect a widespread disruption of cellular communication and structural integrity (@fig-pathway-analysis c). These processes align with established evidence of synaptic disruption and extracellular matrix remodeling in early cognitive decline [@RN49; @RN55; @RN56]. Immune response and glial cell regulation terms were concentrated in this same early transition rather than in advancing disease: the immune response terms fell almost entirely in normal2mci, and glial cell regulation only in normal2mci and normal2incid (@fig-pathway-analysis c). The stable_mci group carried hypoxic responses, which promote pathological protein accumulation and exacerbate memory deficits [@RN50; @RN52], together with the only regulatory-mechanism terms in the analysis. Progression from MCI to incident dementia was uniquely enriched for hormone signaling and for cell migration and organization [@RN57; @RN58; @RN59]. In prevalent dementia, cell-cycle regulation was the only uniquely enriched category, consistent with the recognized role of aberrant cell cycle re-entry in late-stage neurodegeneration [@RN53; @RN54]. Structural, signaling and immune disruption therefore co-occurred at the onset of cognitive decline rather than succeeding one another, giving way to a narrower and more specific set of processes as dementia became established.

At the two ends of the progression — the earliest transition and established dementia — the number of significant CpG sites and the number of enriched biological processes ran in opposite directions. Most of the 403 significant sites (326) belonged to prevalent dementia, yet that group yielded only 22 enriched GO biological processes. Conversely, few sites reached genome-wide significance in any of the four transition groups, yet normal2mci alone yielded 155 enriched processes — more than three times as many as mci2incid (48) and seven times as many as prevalent dementia — of which 140 were unique to it (@fig-pathway-analysis b, @suppdata-GO_top1000). Because the enrichment analysis drew a fixed number of top-ranked CpG sites from every group, the gene sets entering it were of comparable size (@fig-pathway-analysis a), so this contrast is not an artifact of the uneven numbers of genome-wide significant sites. It points instead to heightened biological activity at the onset of cognitive decline, mirroring the early hyperactivation described across the Alzheimer's disease continuum [@RN83].

### Limitations

Several issues should be considered when interpreting these results. Clinical staging carries a degree of uncertainty, particularly at the intermediate MCI stage. Diagnoses in AGES-Reykjavik followed a standardized, adjudicated protocol and were supported by comprehensive surveillance of dementia cases through the fully digitized Icelandic health care records, including nursing homes (see Methods) [@RN1; @RN63]; to limit misclassification further, we counted only study-based diagnoses of MCI. Because cognition was assessed only at the two study examinations, some participants classified as normal2incid may have passed through an unrecorded MCI stage; direct progression from normal cognition to dementia is nonetheless a well-documented trajectory, accounting for close to 40% of converters even in cohorts with repeated annual assessment [@RN87]. The proportions transitioning into MCI and from MCI to dementia were similar to those reported by the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging [@RN90]. Because the stable_mci group includes participants who reverted to normal cognition, and reverters carry a higher subsequent risk of dementia [@RN90], that group is unlikely to be biologically homogeneous. We also did not account for differential mortality across the groups, so we cannot exclude the possibility that some participants in the normal and MCI groups died before reaching a dementia state or had very slowly progressing disease; some of the significant CpG sites may therefore reflect survival rather than dementia risk.

Blood methylation is an indirect surrogate for central nervous system biology, and some transition groups were relatively small, so several group-specific estimates were likely underpowered and require replication in larger cohorts.

The pathway analyses relied on rank-based CpG selection to keep the gene sets comparable across groups, which prioritizes relative rather than absolute significance (see Methods). Because selection was relative, the top-ranked lists for the four transition groups consisted almost entirely of sub-threshold sites — normal2incid contributed a single genome-wide significant site, normal2mci five, mci2incid nine and stable_mci 62 — so the processes enriched in those groups are suggestive and observational. Deeper profiling of the genes linked to those CpG sites is needed. Our comparisons were made relative to the stable normal or the prevalent dementia group, and our results may not generalize to studies whose stable normal group, study design, source population, or mix of dementia groups differs from ours. The associations reported here are observational and do not establish causality.

Together, these findings indicate that blood DNA methylation captures trajectory-specific changes years before clinical dementia, and that the early and late transitions engage distinct biology. That distinction may aid risk stratification and the design of stage-appropriate interventions, rather than defining early disease by extrapolating from late-stage pathology.
